It has been indicated that the narrative, beginning with Mantharā’s entrance and ending with Rāmabhadra’s departure, has been told.
Thereafter— meaning after Rāmabhadra’s departure— he scattered— that is, he cast— [the ashes] into the Gaṅgā.
"I have become [a being]; that is to say, "I have bathed. And the bathing is due to the loathsomeness of entering another's body; or else, "in the Gaṅgā" means on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
By way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*), the word "stayed" (*sthitam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis;

"I have become one who has come" (*āgatyabhūtāsmi*) means that I am connected with the action of coming, i.e., "I have arrived. This is according to the rule for the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group, which includes the *snātvākālaka* group.
Its correctness [is established] by virtue of being included under the word "etc. (*ādi*); or else, it consists of two words:
*āgatya* = having arrived, and *bhūtā* = accomplished; thus the meaning is simply "having arrived. And so Śrī Harṣa says regarding you:—tvayi...
"I have been dispatched by that mountain-king, who is constantly afflicted by love and possessed of pride;
having arrived, I shall become fruitful through your recognition of my intent, O lady who yearns for virtue. (2) "Immediately thereafter"—that is, subsequently; this refers to his departure.
The absence of delay has been indicated. (3) *Anuyuktā* means "questioned";
according to Amarasimha, "anuyoga, pṛcchā, and praśna" all mean "question.
*Putrīyate*, etc. [is explained as follows].
*Putrīyatā* means "desiring a son for oneself"; [it is derived] by *Pāṇini* 3.1.8 (*supa ātmanaḥ kyac*).
The sage is Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. *Kalāḥ* means "parts" or "portions."
One characterized by *guṇa* (virtue) is the *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled). One who is *dhīroddhata* (bold and arrogant) is *dṛpta* (haughty);
as it has been said: "One who abounds in pride and envy, who possesses deceit and egoism, who is treacherous, fierce, and boastful—such a person is described as *dhīroddhata*. (6) Thus.
By this, the essential nature of these two has been described. //1//
"At the edge of the water" is because of the traditional injunction: "One should follow a dear traveler as far as the edge of the forest or the edge of the water.
(7) "Attendants" (*ānuyātrikāḥ*) means those whose purpose is to accompany [the traveler]. (8) "Agitation" (*sambhramaḥ*) arises from devotion toward Rāma.

Regarding the passage beginning with *tīrtvā* and so forth: *dhunī* means "river"; as Amara states, "taṭinī, hrādinī, dhunī. The third case ending in *ātmanā* is used because [the word] belongs to the class beginning with *prakṛti*.
"Niṣparijana" means "without attendants. "Ātaram" refers to the ferry-toll;
"upakṛtavān" means he gave it. (11) "Vyāma" is a specific measure of length; as Amarasimha states: "A vyāma is the horizontal distance between the two outstretched arms with hands extended. (12)

The quality of being graspable by both arms (*vyāmagrāhyatva*) [is mentioned] because of the height of the breasts by the man standing behind. Regarding *udañcadakṣam*: "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ṣac* is applied after *sakthi* and *akṣi* when they denote a limb of one's own body. Regarding *kṛcchrāt* and *kṣaṇam*.
Because of the excessive weight of her breasts. //2//
"Pitiable" means bringing grief; "conduct" is the word understood [from the context].
"Udarka" refers to the fruit of a later time.
[This was done] for the pleasure of Niṣādapati Guha; this [act] consists of complying with his mind.
Courtesy is indeed an ornament.
As it has been said: "That which consists in following the mind [of others] is called courtesy. *Gaṇarātram* means many nights.

*Niśāḥ* (nights): Since the word *gaṇa* is a numeral according to the rule *bahugaṇavatu* etc., the suffix *ac* is applied to the word *rātri* by the rule *ahaḥsarvaika* etc. *Prakṛtayaḥ* = ministers. By that same [rule].
He urges [him] along the very path of Rāma’s deeds;
Jāmbavān’s apprehension is whether [the mission] might be abandoned due to Bharata’s entreaty.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tataśca" and so forth: *tasmin* means on that [Citrakūṭa]. *Chalitaḥ* means deceived; by this, he expresses that his mother was without fault. *Anubandhaḥ* means persistence;
one who possesses this is *anubandhī*, meaning one who is insistent.
Regarding the body, touch (*sparśa*) is what is meant by *spṛṣṭikā*; it has been rejected: "If, beyond this..."
The meaning is that her arrival was forbidden by an oath of this form: "If you have touched my body with the intent to kill, then you shall be bound.
*Bhadrāsana* refers to the royal throne. (19)
"Prosperous" (*ābhyudayika*) means an action whose purpose is prosperity (*abhyudaya*);
the sense is that it has borne fruit because Rāma has not turned back.
This is the limb (*aṅga*) called "Sequence" (*krama*), which consists in the accomplishment of the non-turning back of the noble Rāma, who was the object of [her] anxiety.
As it has been said: "The sequence is the attainment through deliberate reflection" (21).
*Āśauca* means unfitness for ritual action (*karmānarhatva*). *Āsthitasya* means of one who has accepted [the vow]. This is the prohibition regarding weapons.
Because the duties of the castes and stages of life must be abandoned during impurity; and that [impurity] is as follows:
"A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle or weapon, a Vaiśya by his goad or reins, and a Śūdra..."

"Having performed the rites, he may touch the staff" (22)— since this statement by Manu, which declares purification through the touching of water and other substances, effectively indicates that during the period of impurity one is generally unfit to touch vehicles and the like.

That [transgression] in which the cessation of misfortune occurs immediately upon its commission is *ātipātika*; the suffix *ṭhak* is used here in its own sense (*svārthika*), and there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both parts of the compound according to the rule for the *anuśatikādi* group. Thus, it means "immediate purification."
"Regarding the duties of protecting the earth for kings and those dispatched by them," according to the statement of Yājñavalkya (25),
[the king's duty] was momentarily suspended by execution; yet, compared to grief, it is but a long day.
In that [context], it is "dīrghāhnī" (a long day); this is according to the rule *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.28).
The suffix *ṅīp* [is applied]. That which occurs after the body is "aurdhvadaihikī"; that is what is meant.
The suffix *ṭhak* is added by the rule *ūrdhvadehācca* (Pāṇini 4.3.60);
the vowel lengthening of both members of the compound occurs because it belongs to the *anuśatikādi* group.

*Ritual action* refers to acts such as the offering of *tilāñjali*. One who "sucks with the fist" is a *muṣṭindhaya*; the suffix *khaś* is applied here according to the rule *nāḍīmuṣṭyośca* (Pāṇini 3.2.30). *The undertaking of fickleness* is the obstruction of the movement of the sun.

Regarding the phrase "with an auspicious jar": at the time of sleep for kings, a full jar is placed nearby for the purpose of warding off bad dreams; that is to say, [the jar] which slew Vātāpin. (31)

"Sanāthām" means "the southern forest," for Agastya dwells in the southern direction. Regarding the form "pratiṣṭhamāne," the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) affix is applied according to the rule beginning with "samava-pra."

"Rakṣobhicāra," and so forth. The breast [of Rāvaṇa] became a vessel for the *caru* (sacrificial porridge) used for the malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) against Rāvaṇa because, by deluding him, it was the cause of his destruction. "Made of *aiṣīka*" means produced from *iṣīkā* reeds; [it is formed] by that...

The suffix *ṭhak* [is applied] in the sense of "produced from" (*nirvṛtta*). *Iṣīkāḥ* refers to a specific kind of grass. *Adhikṛtya* means "having taken as the subject" or "having adopted. In the word *akṣṇā*, the third case ending is used according to the rule *yenāṅgavikāraḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.20). //3//
"In due order": Sutīkṣṇa was the brother of Agastya. //4//

*Kāmukī* means one who desires to sport (*riraṃsuḥ*); the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule beginning with "from *jānapada*" (Pāṇini 4.1.42). *Rasam* means both poison and pleasure; as it is said: "In the sense of erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth, poison, potency, quality, passion, and liquid..."
"Rasa" [is defined] by Amarasimha as [the essence]. That which is [the malice], namely the desire to kill (*jighāṃsā*), directed toward Rāma who was conceived as a husband.
"Pātakavatī" means she conceived of an expiation for the sin; that is to say, she performed the penance. The sense is that the appropriate punishment has been incurred.
*Kanda* is the place where a sprout arises. *Pratipannam* means "what has been attained"?
That which is being attained is what is meant by "pratipannam"—this is the ellipsis.
*Prahatam* means "crushed. Because they share a single purpose with Virādha, [it refers] to that very [place].
"Going"; by this, the misfortune of Vālin is also indicated— meaning, "Are they dead?"—
with apprehension, even before the accomplishment of his own purpose.
Jāmbavān’s apprehension was that a calamity would befall the noble Rāma from Rāvaṇa, rooted in the humiliation of Śūrpaṇakhā.
"Prarūḍha" means sprouted.
"Of oneself," the ellipsis is "a particular state of being overcome. "Even without words" means even without speech.
"Laghūtthāna" means a swift departure.

He explains this very point with the words "by the descendant of Ikṣvāku," and so forth. The form [Aikṣvāka] is derived as an irregular formation (nipāta) according to the rule beginning with "dāṇḍināyana.
"Śāśvatika" means that which has arisen repeatedly; [this refers to the battle] because of the slaying of Tāṭakā and others.
The state [of being] is as follows: these, beginning with *khara*. *Alambhūṣṇuḥ* means "capable";
by the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *glājisthaśca gsnuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.139), the suffix *gsnu* is also applied to the root *bhū*. (40)

This is the ornament called "Investigation" (vicāra), which consists of the delineation of the slaying of Tāṭakā and other such acts as the means for accomplishing the objective of Rāmabhadra, even though that objective is of the nature of a calamity.
As it has been said: "Inquiry (vicāra), however, is the description of many means for that which is to be accomplished by a single [method]. (41) //5//

*Sandhukṣaṇam* means increasing; the verbal root is *dhukṣa* in the sense of "kindling" (DhP 4.2). The intended meaning is that, because [the fire] has already arrived, one desires to kindle it (*sandhitsati*).

"Mine," and so forth: "the pupil's son" indicates his obedience; "the universal monarch" indicates his worthiness as an object of great respect; and "Lakṣmaṇa’s friend" indicates that his word is to be accepted by Rāma.
He states the causal complex for the task at hand:
"bring near"—that is, cause to reach; the words "into the presence of Rāma" are to be supplied.
Regarding the term "far-sighted": vultures indeed possess keen vision; as it has been said:

Baṅgasena said: "Sulfate of copper (*tuttha*) that has been repeatedly heated and then poured into cow urine, goat's milk, sour gruel (*amlakāñjika*), woman’s breast milk, clarified butter, poison, and honey—that shall make a man’s eye equal to Garuḍa. (43) Thus [he spoke]. *Upalabheta* means "one would see."
From "Starting from here" up to "we too shall practice this very [path]" (44), there is the ornament called *siddhi* (attainment), because it consists in the occurrence of what was not anticipated.
As it has been said: "Attainment (*siddhi*) is the union with a desired object that occurs unexpectedly. (45)
"Are seen," and so forth. *Prāgbhāraḥ* means a mass or heap. Sand (*sikatā*) is indeed difficult to traverse;
for this very reason, it is said "with difficulty" (*kṛcchrāt*). *Lubdhakāḥ* means hunters (*vyādhāḥ*).
"By continuous" means by those falling without interruption. "Without fear" refers to the absence of fear regarding the tracks, because hunters follow the footprints. //6//
"How much less," [the word] "has come" being understood as the ellipsis;
"reception" refers to inquiries concerning one's welfare and so forth;
"for now" indicates being preoccupied with other duties; "dear Rāmabhadra" is said out of brotherly affection toward Daśaratha.
The word "child" (*vatsa*) is used because he is equal to a son.
"This very [thing]" refers back to the account of Rāvaṇa. Regarding "was led," and so forth: the deer itself was the disguise. "Being afraid," and so forth.
The absence of the augment *num* is due to the rule *nābhyastāc chatuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.78). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "This Rāvaṇa, therefore, manifests his own form."
From this point up to the end of the passage, "Jaṭāyu is a doer of cruel deeds" (47), is the dramatic element named *adhibala* because it consists of deception;
as it has been said: "*adhibala* is overreaching. (48) //7//
"O noble son"—the noble one is the father-in-law; "son" means the husband. "This wicked man goes"—the construction is: "Where is he going? //8//
"Vadhūṭīm," and so forth: belonging to the Ikṣvāku lineage, *vadhūṭīm* means a young woman; for "a *vadhūṭī* and a *ciraṇṭī* are both in their second stage of life."
"Two women," according to the *Abhidhānaratnamālā* (49).
For this very reason, there is impurity through contact with another man.

Because [offending] children and the elderly does not bring about fault. "Bhavataḥ" means of you, the inferior one; the sense is that the inferior person rejoices in evil. However, they too are "gurus," meaning those who promote right conduct. Seven.
The *brahmās* are Marīci and the others; as it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*: "The one of great splendor created seven: Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasiṣṭha."
Those belonging to the mind.

"These seven are the Brahmas; this is the certainty established in the Purāṇas. (50) Thus [ends the passage]. These words, spoken by Pulastya and others, were not counted—that is, they were not taken into account—for the sake of Rāvaṇa's embarrassment.
They have been deliberated upon; the sense is that this is not suitable for one of noble lineage. //9//
*Apaśada* means base or low-born.
*Āmiṣa* refers to an object of enjoyment, and specifically to meat, because vultures feed upon it; by the term "old vulture," he expresses their lack of capability. Having snatched away—
"Having taken [it] by force"—the word "kila" expresses a derisive remark prompted by [his] lack of power. //10//
"Arms like branches," and so forth. *Andhambhaviṣṇuḥ* means "becoming blind"; [the suffix] *khiṣṇuc* is applied by the rule *kartari bhuvaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.57).
The meaning is "deluded. For one who is intoxicated becomes deluded.
Being reviled as "thief-maker" (*coraṅkāram*).

The root *kṛñ* has the sense of uttering (*uccāraṇa*); having uttered the word "thief" (*cora*), the meaning is that he is being censured as "you are a thief. The underlying intention is that for one who is capable, it is improper to withdraw without having discharged the charge. [According to the rule] *karmaṇyākrośe kṛñaḥ khamuñ*, the sense of the sentence is the object (*karman*). *Avaskāraḥ* means with joy (*harṣeṇa*).
The rending of the earth;
(56) the augment *suṭ* is applied by the rule "apāccatuṣpāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.142). For this very reason, there is the expression "playful" (*kelī*).
This is a rash act (*sāhasa*) because it involves an activity that disregards one's own life.
The *nāma* is a sub-division (*upāṅga*) of the *sandhi*; as it has been said: "An act performed regardless of one's own life is *sāhasa* (recklessness).

Regarding the term *viṣkambha*: it is so called because it provides a concise indication (*sūcana*) of what has already occurred, such as the slaying of Virādha, and what is yet to occur, such as the alliance with Sugrīva and the battle with Rāvaṇa; furthermore, its purity (*śuddhatva*) arises from its being enacted by a superior character (*uttama-pātra*).
"Difficult to ward off," and so forth: anger arises from being deceived; grief from the apprehension of Sītā’s destruction; and shame from the abduction of his wife.
Because of the intensity of anger and other such states, which are difficult to restrain and fierce, [the path] is "thick" (*gahana*), meaning difficult to enter. "Vitarka" means ripening.
"Itikartavyatā" means what ought to be done. "Anaupayika" means devoid of means; [it is derived from] "upāya..."
The suffix *ṭhak* in the word *hrasvatvam* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). The remedy, however, is far off; the point is that there is not even an instructor of the means [to it].
He says this very thing with the words beginning "that such... (*tattādṛg* etc.). Deception: "led far away" (*nīto dūram*).
This is stated in the verse beginning with "ityādi. "Dhūmāyamānaḥ" means becoming possessed of smoke—that is, being smoky.
Since the word *lohita* belongs to the class of words known as *ākṛtigaṇa*, the suffix *kyaṣ* is applied [to form *dhūmāyate*].
In its functional application (*vṛtti*), the word *dhūma* refers to that which possesses smoke.

This is due to the inherent nature of the power of words. (62) By this, the manifestation of anger, which is of the nature of a blazing fire, is indicated hereafter; for that which has been smoldering as smoke indeed blazes up. This is shown by the half-uttered speech born of anger, because its syllables have been lost.
"Distraught" means devoid of meaning; "he does not attain" means he does not speak it in its entirety.
"Father" is an expression used for the sake of consolation regarding the report of his life.
The limit (*paryanta*) is the conclusion, that is to say, death;
she whose numbness born of grief was destroyed by the fire of anger produced by the recollection of Jaṭāyu’s death. As it has been said: "And grief..."

"By means of the fierce and the peaceful" (63); the word "is concealed" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Here, by the word "fierce," anger is indicated, because it is emotion itself that conceals [other] emotions (64). In the bow...
"It rests" means that it serves as a means of remedy; this is the intended sense.
The gazing at the bow is an ensuant emotion (*anubhāva*) of anger.
As it has been said: "Squeezing the hands, trembling of the limbs, and waiting for a weapon. (65) //12//
In order to divert Rāma’s dejection born of anger by means of a description of the forest, he says: "This way, this way," and so forth.
The exhortation, "O slayer of Mārīca," is for the purpose of obscuring his grief.
"Downward" means toward the south. Rāma’s ears [were directed] due to being overcome by anger.
"From which family," and so forth. "The collection of arms" refers to military force; in terms of family and other such qualities, there is no one equal to you in either the past or the future.

But regarding the present moment, the sense is "from where?"— that is, from where has this long-standing confusion of directions come to you who are such as you are? For the path by which you have gone— that is,
by way of deception—
is not the path of heroes.
Even one who is confused about the directions goes by a wrong path. //13//
"By a smile born of weariness, due to both the separation from his beloved and the apprehension of fear from Rāvaṇa.
Regarding "the Siddhas," etc.:
*siddhāḥ* refers to a particular class of divine beings (*devayoni*). "Excluding Pulastya" means having set aside Pulastya.

The suffix *ṇamul* is used in the sense of "and in the second [case]" (Pāṇini 3.4.26). Its absence of a smile is due to the embarrassment caused by the misconduct of his great-grandson. "Existing in all directions" (*viṣvagvṛtti*) means existing in the four cardinal points;
for this very reason, it is unfit for the bowing down prompted by shame, because when one head is bent, another head would rise up.
"Caturmukhī" [is used] in the singular because it is a collective dvigu compound.

(14) (68) Regarding "anudhyāya" (having meditated upon): "Sītām" (Sītā) is the ellipsis. Here, meditation is the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) of sorrow (*śoka*), which is the *sthāyibhāva* (permanent emotion) of *karuṇa* (pathos); [as in the verse: "O beloved..."
"O Princess of Videha!
(69)—this recollection of her qualities is the *uddīpana-vibhāva* (the excitant cause). *Saṃvaraṇam* means concealment;
[it refers to] his own status as a supreme hero (*uttama-nāyaka*).

The ellipsis (*iti śeṣaḥ*) refers to "of the levity" indicated by the vocal action in the form of the sound *hā*, which is prompted by the state of being a middling hero; as it has been said: "Even compassion is divided into three kinds—born of mental, vocal, and physical actions—and this [levity] occurs respectively in the superior, middling, and inferior [heroes]."

"...is produced. (70) And: "The syllable *hā*, weeping, crying out, lamenting, speaking piteously, calling from afar, and wailing—this is known as the pathetic (*karuṇa*) vocal [sentiment]. (71) [And] dancing...
By the power of his fortitude, such as the serenity of his countenance and so forth;
"O Noble One," etc.;
*abhiṣaṅga* means grief. "Who is this? means of what kind? "It is marvelous."
This is an expression of excessive grief. "Persons such as you" means those who are *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled).
The omission of the word "you" (*bhavantam*) is out of modesty. By this, Rāma's status as the *ālambana-vibhāva* (the objective basis of emotion) is stated.
As it has been said: "The substratum (ālambana) is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of rasa.

(72) The word *api* implies contradiction; the sense is that it is contradictory for grief (*śoka*), which has a base object as its substratum, to reside in a noble and exalted (*dhīrodātta*) character. [For] the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*), whose essence is grief, has women, base persons, and so forth as its natural objects.
"It is taught that this [sorrow] arises from the loss of what is desired, from the attainment of what is undesired, and from fate. (73) Herein,
[the first type is] that born from the loss of what is desired.
"Falls," and so forth. "In calamity" means in grief. "By fate" conceals the fact that [the grief] arises from the loss of a desired object through misfortune.
"In a nature that tears asunder" means having a disposition toward rending; the mind is the agent.
*Saṃvarmayati* means he arms himself with armor; the suffix *ṇic* is applied to the word *varman* in the sense of "arming" according to the rule beginning with *satyāpapāśa*.
*Vajreṇa* means by means of a diamond-like armor; this is said because grief can only be warded off by fortitude. "This is the grief of the noble... [is the remainder].
"Even when deeply rooted, it is generally pacified by fortitude through the cultivation of other mental states established elsewhere, rather than those residing within oneself. (75)
Thus //15//

"Exhaling" refers to long and hot sighs and so forth, which are the expressive manifestations (*anubhāva*) of grief directed toward a supreme object; as it has been said: "the non-attention to external objects."
The lengthening of inhalation and exhalation;
and dejection regarding equanimity, clothing, grooming of the limbs, and so forth.
Non-recognition of what has been experienced, instability of mind, detachment from all objects,
lack of attachment toward those who are dear, and gazing into space.
"The compassionate one is known as mental" (76). Thus, it has already been shown previously that for the highest [type of person], the compassionate one is mental. (77)
"Born together," and so forth. "Submissive" (*vaśaṃvadāḥ*) means favorable; [according to Pāṇini 3.2.38] *khac* is added to the root *vad* when preceded by *priya* or *vaśa*.
"Restrained" (*niyantritāḥ*) means paralyzed. The sense is that anger and grief are to be checked by fortitude, but not shame arising from public censure. //16//
He introduces another topic to divert her modesty, beginning with "This," and so forth.
*Siddhakṣetra* means a place free from obstacles for performing austerities.

"This one is broken," and so forth. How is it? In what manner does it exist? That is to say, it is shattered. "Apaskiramāṇāḥ" means tearing [the ground] out of joy; for [the rule] states: "The root *kṛ* [is used] in the senses of joy, livelihood, and making a lair."
The form *vaktavyam* is in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
*Bhaṅgurāḥ* means crooked;
*troṭiḥ* means a beak.
According to Amarasimha, "Cañcu and stroṭi are both feminine";
by these [beaks], the joints and bonds were severed.

In this instance, because the sorrow [of the speaker] is not overwhelmed by either similar or dissimilar factors— namely, by grief and anger, which are respectively ignited by the words *tāta* and *rāvaṇa*— it subsequently functions as a rasa.

Because it is stated that "it ripens" and because it persists until that point, he says— showing their subordinate status in order to highlight the permanence [of the emotion]— Rāma (with compassion): "Alas!"

Regarding "Sīradhvaja" and so forth, it has been said: "That which exists as long as the aesthetic flavor (rasa) persists, whose form is not eclipsed by those of its own or different classes, is the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva)."
Thus it has been stated.
(82) The fact that [the hero's] power is not disregarded is due to the employment of the word *hā*.
By the phrase "O fortunate one," she implies: "We are unfortunate, for we do not behold such valor of his."
Such is the intended meaning. //17//
"Having supported" means having relied upon; reliance [is mentioned] because there is an absence of capacity for physical activity or stability.
By this form of manifestation, that which is called "sickness"—characterized by a lack of vitality—is indicated as a transitory emotion (*sañcāribhāva*) directed toward grief.
As it has been said: "Exhaustion here [is defined] as the loss of vitality caused by mental anguish, physical disease, old age, thirst, exertion, sexual intercourse, and so forth;
it consists of the emaciation of the limbs and of speech and action. (83) In this context, the activity of the limbs is emaciated.
"Great is the fault," and so forth. The sense is that if grief becomes excessive, it is difficult to restrain.

"Elsewhere" (*anyataḥ*) means in another state of being; the suffix *-tasi* is used here in place of all case endings. "I extend"—the word "mental activity" (*manovṛtti*) is to be supplied as the object. Here, regarding grief...
Because it consists of mere emotion (*bhāva*), it is concealed by another emotion in the form of pleasure produced by the sight of a female dancer’s performance;
however, in the state of *rasa*, it is concealed by *rasa* itself. As he will say: "But by what other *rasa* is this *rasa* obscured? (84). It is not merely by this much...
The refutation of permanence [is established] because of arising again;
"Vindhya," etc.;
"the maiden's inner apartments" refers to the young girls (by metaphorical usage), and [this implies] their state of maidenhood.
Because it originates from that [word], its neuter gender follows from its fixed gender. "Vetasvatībhiḥ" means "by those possessing many reeds";
[this is formed] by the rule: *kumudanaḍavetasebhyo ḍmatup*. (85)
*Tāuryatrikam* refers to dance, song, and instrumental music; as Amarasimha states: "The *tāuryatrika* consists of dance, song, and instrumental music" (86).
*Guṇanikām* means practice. The dance is performed by the movement of the waves.
The singing is provided by the humming of bees clinging to the excellent flowers on its banks;
the instrumental music is the sound of the flood of water; and the mention of training in dancing and other arts is due to her being a princess. //18//

"Kumudavana," and so forth. *Viśāya* means sleeping by turns; [as stated in the rule: "The root *śī* [takes the suffix *ghañ*] after the prefixes *vi-* and *upa-* when meaning 'turning' (paryāya). (Pāṇini 3.3.39).

Thus, the suffix *ghañ* [is applied]. *Yāmikāḥ* refers to the soldiers who protect the king and others by means of alternating watches (*paryāya-bodha*); from the word *yāma*, the suffix *ṭhak* is added according to the rule "he protects" (Pāṇini 4.4.33).
This too is because it belongs to the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*). *Karṇatālaḥ* means the sound of the ears and the sound of the clapping of hands (*tāla*).

By means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*): [the phrase] "mukharā" (resonant) refers to the production of song; and due to the delusion that the sound of clouds was the *tāla* of an elephant's ear, there is dancing. //19//
"Here," and so forth. "Wild buffaloes" refers to those found in the forest; their tossing of stones occurs during the rainy season due to excessive rut.

And this [tree] is both pregnant and a *rohit*; the compound is formed as "pregnant four-footed animal" (*catuṣpādo garbhiṇyā*) according to rule 89; because it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), [the feminine suffix is elided].
The word *rohi* is placed first [in the compound].
(90) Due to the falling of stones that have tumbled from the upper slopes (*adhityakā*), the female deer dwelling on the lower slopes (*upatyakā*)—
The meaning is that they perish. *Hikkā* is a specific sound like the cry of a bear;
the expression "hikkā" arises because bears become intoxicated during the rainy season (*prāvṛṣ*).

"Vanāntāḥ" means the very forms of the forest; according to the *Amaraśeṣa*, "antaḥ" [is used] in the senses of "end," "death," and "essential nature. (20) (91) [The phrase] "with compassionate tears" [is explained as follows].
Due to the predominance of the seasonal phenomena (*ṛtudharma*) as excitants (*uddīpanavibhāva*), there is a description of a particular state of grief.
Regarding the phrase "at every turn" (*pratiparisaram*) and so forth:
*parisara* means a location or region.
Regarding "śikhaṇḍabhṛtām" (of the peacock pairs): the term "pumān striyā" (Pāṇini 1.2.67) applies as a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member). "Arghaḥ" means esteem or honor.
"Yathāmilitam" means not deviating from the manner in which they have met; [it is used] in the sense of "attainment" (niṣṭhā).
It is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "yathā-sādṛśye. Honey is drunk by pairs of bees having met together.

The sense is: "because of its abundance. So that it may be thus, [the mountain] has peaks covered with clouds and is garlanded. "Priyaṅkaraṇīḥ" means those things which serve as the means for bringing about what is dear.
By the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.140] *āḍhyādi-sūtra*, the suffix *khyun* is applied.
During the rainy season, the emergence of embryos occurs in female snakes;
this has been stated in the *Viṣasārasamuccaya*: "Of serpents..."
"Likewise, there may be conception in Āṣāḍha and in Śrāvaṇa as well.
(96) Thus, by describing the sexual union of the couple, Rāma’s extreme grief is indicated. //21//

He says that very thing with the words "this" and so forth. The instrumental case in *srastaiḥ* is used in the sense of a qualifying characteristic (*upalakṣaṇe*). The emotion (*bhāva*) of sorrow (*śoka*), when it is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) permeated by the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors, transforms into the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of pathos (*karuṇarasa*).

As it has been said: "The permanent emotion (sthāyībhāva), when brought to a state of relish through the determinants (vibhāvas), the consequents (anubhāvas), the involuntary physical states (sāttvikas), and the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhis), is known as rasa. (98)

Thus: regarding the fact that sorrow (*śoka*) is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*), it is said: "Sorrow, when brought to a state of aesthetic relish (*rasatva*) by the audience, becomes the pathetic sentiment" (99). Its objective basis (*ālambana*) is Rāma, [as indicated by the thought]: "He makes even those like you a vessel [for his grief]" (100).

Because it has been stated previously: "O beloved, daughter of the King of Videha"—thus, the recollection of her qualities, the rainy season, and so forth, are the excitant determinants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*); the consequent determinants (*anubhāva*) are paleness of complexion and dryness of the mouth.

And there are the previously mentioned [symptoms] of suppressed weeping, meditation, and sighing. Regarding that, with reference to grief (*śoka*), it is said: "In that state, the physical manifestations (*ceṣṭā*) are pallor, the rising of tears, and dryness of the mouth."

"Stupor, sighing, and so forth" (103). Among these, *vaisvarya* (change of voice) and *bāṣpa* (tears) are *sāttvika* [emotions]; the transitory states (*sañcāribhāvas*) are: delusion (*moha*), indicated by the loss of memory;
despondency (*nirveda*), indicated by sighing; and exhaustion (*glāni*), indicated by the drooping of the limbs.

There is languor and exhaustion, as well as a stupor that produces a state of helplessness, indicated by the words, "Supported by Lakṣmaṇa, he remains with his eyes closed" (104). Thus it has been said:
Having introduced the state of insensibility (*jāḍya*), [the text says]: "In that state, there is the absence of blinking, lack of hearing, helplessness, silence, and so forth" (105).
This is indicated by lamentation and cries of "Alas! (*hāhākāra*).
And there is insanity;

as it has been said: "Insanity is a derangement of the mind resulting from separation, the loss of what is desired, and so forth. However, the behaviors [occurring] in that which arises from separation are as follows:"
"Running about and lamentation [occur]. (106) Regarding the transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) associated with *sāttvika* [emotions] in the context of grief (*śoka*), Bhoja states:

"In that regard, there are eight *sāttvika* [states]: torpor (*jāḍya*), despondency (*nirveda*), languor (*glāni*), dejection (*dīnatā*), lethargy (*ālasya*), forgetfulness (*apasmṛti*), illness (*vyādhi*), and delusion (*moha*), among others, which are transitory mental states. (107)

"But by what," and so forth. "Is obscured" means it is covered; and its quality of being an obscuring agent is because it has been stated: "Even a preceding rasa, when complete, obscures another rasa" (108).
The agent is the subsequent rasa, and the preceding rasa is the object.
Even in that case, since it is the *raudra* (furious) rasa that obscures the *karuṇa* (compassionate) rasa, it is that very one which has been introduced.
As it has been said: "And grief [is intensified] by the fierce and the peaceful" (110).

And that [grief] arises from the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) called anger—a conflagration of the mind born from the contempt for one's own qualities, consisting of an assault previously committed by Kabandha, as indicated by Guha’s words beginning with, "Ah, you sinner, Kabandha! (111).
As it has been said: "Krodha (anger) is described as the inflaming of the mind through killing, contempt, and so forth" (112);
and this [anger] is inferred from the transitory state (*sañcāribhāva*) known as *sambhrama* (agitation), which is synonymous with *āvega* (alarm) and is centered on the object of passion (*rāma*).

Regarding that, it has been said concerning anger: "Agitation, pride, indignation, ferocity, delusion, and so forth are the transitory emotions" (113). From this point onward, "a great assault by Vālī is anticipated" (114).
The limb named *udvega* (agitation) is the form of fear caused by an enemy;
as it has been said: "Agitation is fear produced by an enemy" (115).
[This refers to] the headless trunk (*kabandha*) named Danu, because its head is situated within its chest.
It is designated as such because it has the form of a headless trunk (*kabandha*).
"Engaging in strife" (*kalahāyamāna*) means performing a quarrel, that is, a battle;
[this refers to the category] "sound-enmity" (*śabdavaira*).
By such [expressions] as "kyaṅ"; according to Amarasimha, "kalahāsphoṭasaṃyugāḥ" [means quarrels, slapping, and battles].
[The phrase] "it is heard like Guha" is [conveyed] by means of *dhvani* (suggestion).
The word *guha* means "it is inferred"; the particle *iva* expresses deliberation (*vitarka*). *Chala* means deception.
*Abhyupapadyasva* means "favor" or "show kindness"; for it is said that "favor (*abhyupapatti*) is assistance (*anugraha*). (119)
Thus says Amara.
Rāma (with pathos): "O Goddess of perverse character," and so forth. This is merely a subversion of the *karuṇa* rasa, not a loss of its essential nature;
for [the pathos is maintained] by the dispatching of Lakṣmaṇa to slay Kabandha.
Because of the departure of anger— which acts as an obstruction— due to the conception of a remedy,
yet because it manifests once again, she is "of crooked character" (*vāmaśīlā*), that is, of a perverse nature; by this, a lovers' quarrel is indicated.
"Viśva... and so forth. She is the witness to all secrets.
He says that very thing with the words "svavapuṣi" and so forth. "By herself" (svena) means by her own self (ātmanā).
By saying "in secret" (rahasi), he indicates the absence of any conscious witness. Thus.

Regarding the word *bhīṣitāyāḥ*: by this it is stated that there was merely a verbal threat, and not the actual making of nail-marks; for this very reason, since the fear arises from a mere cause, the augment *ṣuk* is applied according to the rule *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* (Pāṇini 7.3.40). And as for the fear...
Due to the imposition of shamelessness;
"smaraparimalasya" means of the fragrance of passion, i.e., of sexual union; "mudrā" means restraint, and upon its breaking; "sarvaṃsahāyāḥ" means of the patient one (the earth).

The suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *pūḥsarvayordārisahoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.41). The word *te* means "you"; the genitive case is used here according to the rule *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.52). By this, it is stated that the means of appeasing one who is angry consists in generating a different form and sentiment (*rasa*) characterized by the terrifying (*bhayānaka*). [This is done] through conciliation (*sāman*), dissension (*bheda*), and so forth.
For it has been said: "By means of generosity, compassion, equanimity, and other such flavors. (123) //23//

"Vinetā," and so forth. "Durgatva" (the state of being a fortress) arises from warding off the afflictions caused by arrogant *rakṣas* demons. Regarding weapons (*astrāṇām*), their nature is to destroy the sins that bring about rebirth as a *rakṣas*. "Avikalam" means free from obstacles (*nirvighnam*).
This is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇam*); the meaning is that there is no obstacle in the form of a curse due to having been struck by Lakṣmaṇa’s arrow.
(124) *Upātiṣṭhata* means "he attained"; the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is used according to the rule *upād devapūjā-* (Pāṇini 1.3.25). (125) //24//

"The paths leading to the gods" refers to that path by which the doers of meritorious deeds travel; it is the northern course of the sun. This is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "That which is north of the Nāgavīthī..."
"And south of the Seven Sages [is the path]; that which is north of Savitṛ is known as the path of the gods (devayāna). (126) Thus; each of these is called the Nāgavīthī.
In the midst of the three paths— divided into three types and known as Vaiśvānara, Jāradgava, and Airāvata— that path which is called Airāvata.
Its intermediate paths are these:
Airāvatī and Mṛgavīthī.
And the Nāgavīthī [path] ends toward the north; as it is said in that very same work: "The Jāradgava station is in the middle, and likewise Airāvata is to the north; Vaiśvānara is to the south."
Thus it has been taught according to reality: "Airāvatī, Mṛgī, and Nāgavīthī—this [is the path]. (128)
And [it is said], "in three ways" (129), and "the drum," etc. Kapīśvara is Vālī;
he has been seen by you.

*Kaṅkāla* refers to the bones of the body; as Amarasimha states: "The word *kaṅkāla* may denote the bone of the body" (1.3.130). *Kūṭa* means a heap or collection; [as in the verse]: "In the sense of illusion (*māyā*), immovability, and a machine..."
According to Amara: "The word *kūṭa* is used in the masculine for heaps of deceit and falsehoods; it is neuter for an iron mace, a mountain peak, and a plowshare. (131) //25//
*Abhiyoga* means encountering [an enemy] with the intent to kill. "Born on account of that" refers to Vālin’s vow: "Whoever throws down the drum-case shall be put to death by me. This is the sense.
"How much less," then? The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the dative case, meaning "for what purpose";
the answer to this is "in order to honor. Or it may be taken as the ablative case. (132)
Because he was carrying Sugrīva’s gift in his hands, the phrase "from the presence of Sugrīva" is implied by the subsequent meaning. Yojanabāhu is Kabandha,
so called because his arms were a yojana in length.
A *vyomayāna* is a *vimāna*; as Amarasimha states: "The word *vimāna* is masculine or neuter, meaning a celestial vehicle (*vyomayāna*)" (verse 133).
"What would happen? = "What great calamity would occur?"—the word "of Sītā" (*sītāyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the object.
"To honor" (*sabhājayitum*) = "to serve"; according to Amarasimha, "joy and honoring" (*ānandana-sabhājane*) [are the meanings of *sabhāja*].
*Prābhṛtam* means a gift or an offering; as Amarasimha states: "A *prābhṛta*, however, is a presentation (*pradeśana*) or an offering (*upāyana*)" (135).

In the expression "he offers to Rāma," there is an absence of the status of recipient (*sampradāna*) because, according to the rule "the mention of the action must be made" (Pāṇini 1.4.32), there is an intention to express a general relationship rather than a specific recipient.
"Only the upper garment remains": among those belonging to you, only the upper garment is seen, and nothing else; that is to say, this is perceived solely through your form.
This is indicated by the phrase beginning with "with eyes closed," and so forth.

This is a statement in the *sāttvika* mode characterized by fainting (*pralaya*); according to Amara, "fainting is the loss of all movement" (137). This should be understood in light of Rāma’s state of helplessness. He himself reflects upon Sugrīva’s inquiry after his welfare and so forth, beginning with the words, "O friend, King of the Niṣādas," etc.
"Vārttam" means the absence of mental affliction; according to Amarasimha, "vārttam" is used in the senses of "well-being" and "health. "Anuyuñjāne" means while he is questioning [her].
The sense is that by means of inquiry into your welfare, her misfortune will depart.

Upon seeing the upper garment, he remembers Rāvaṇa’s arrogance and says, beginning with "jānan" (knowing): "naḥ" means me; according to the rule "asmado dvayośca," the plural is used for the singular;
"knowing me"—the ellipsis being "to be powerless"; [of] himself...

And [the word] *dhīratām* (steadfastness). The indeclinable *astu* is used in the sense of acceptance preceded by resentment; as Vardhamāna states: "The word *astu* is used in the senses of prohibition, resentment, and acceptance. (141)
He says that very thing: "Candrāpīḍam," and so forth.

The word *hi* indicates a reason. It refers to both her own agency in cutting [the hair] and her fortitude. Alternatively, it means "even while knowing her to be our beloved," as expressed in the passage beginning with: "She who was placed in the heart by Paulastya himself, the ruler of the three worlds" (142).

The sense is that he himself has already effectively vowed to abduct Sītā; or alternatively, it means knowing full well his own invulnerability, since even the severing of his head would cause him no harm.
"Śirodāma" means a garland of heads; it also flashes forth as "the garland of Śiva’s head.
It refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of gathering flowers with one's own hands for the purpose of worshipping Śiva. "Aṭavī" [means] the forest.
Even though it was severed, it indicates that it will grow back again. *Vṛtaḥ* means accepted.
"For one who seizes his wife, an assailant, the punishment is indeed the cutting off of the head;
yet that does not hinder him, because [the head] is made by the Candrahāsa sword itself through my arrows."
"Nothing more than this is done"—fie on such useless arrows!
This is the meditative composure born of world-weariness when the virtuous have fallen onto the path of the wicked. //26//
"Forest-dwellers" (*vanaukasaḥ*) refers to monkeys (*vānarāḥ*), according to Amara: "The monkey, the *kīśa*, and the forest-dweller. (143) This statement is made with reference to Sugrīva.
"They long for" (*anurudhyante*) means they desire. (144) "How? means: what should be done? What should be accepted?
The sense is "or not. Alternatively—the meaning is: how so? What is the reason for compliance?
By the words beginning with "What is being said," [the author] addresses both positions.
He states "kinsman" (*bāndhava*) as the subsequent term: *sanābhi* means a relative; *prabhava* means a father.

Alternatively, there are two further explanations: either that one must indeed be connected with a kinsman, or that one desires to go together [with him] because of sharing the same suffering through kinship (*bandhutva*). This is for the purpose of seeing.

The designation *sampradāna* (recipient) applies here by the rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.36); and the longing [of the king] arises from the recollection of her great benevolence, which was evoked by his seeing her upper garment. [This explains the phrase] "performing," and so forth.
*Anūpe* means a region abounding in water; Amarasimha states: "That which abounds in water is *anūpa*" (146);
[the suffix] *ū* is applied after *anu* when denoting a location (147).
Thus, the vowel *a* of the word *ap* [becomes] *u*.

"Laughing" (*prahasana*) refers to the blossoming of flowers; because it is always in flower due to its proximity to water (*anūpatva*), there is constant dancing of peacocks through the delusion that it is the rainy season.
[This applies to] the cooing of pigeons.
The Śabarī’s joy arises from the similarity of their humming, and there is the description of the rose-apple grove as being "pulsating with horripilation. //27//
"Samantāt," and so forth. "Laharyāḥ" means by means of skill in leaping over the flow of waves produced by the wind.
Swiftly turning back, the wind from Lake Pampā—
ignorance and so forth— is the root of delusion.
The manifestation of a hundred Vaidehīs occurs because its fundamental mode of activity conforms to the continuous remembrance [of her];
"supporting the hand" means assistance; and of the winds possessing qualities such as coolness, [there is the scent] of forests.
This was stated in this way precisely because it serves as an illuminator. //28//
"Out of fear," and so forth. "Fear" arises from the sight of the Kirātas. "Fled" means run away.
"Wounded" means broken or afflicted with pain; for this very reason, she was "muttering 'enough, enough,'" speaking indistinctly due to being overwhelmed by suffering.
The word *alam* signifies prohibition; as Amarasimha states: "The word *alam* denotes ornamentation, sufficiency, capability, and warding off. (149)
The verbal root *mlecch* means "an indistinct sound. Even before hearing these words, the arrows that had been aimed—that is, discharged—did not miss the target; they did not fail.
They failed;
they did not pierce the target. "The heart missed" means it failed;
the sense is that there was regret.
In the reading *praṇihitam*— the mind was sent forth even before the discharge of the arrow, because it is impossible for that which is unknown to be a target.
The offense could be rectified,
but once the arrows had gone, they could not be withdrawn, even by the speed of thought.
This is an exaggeration (atiśayokti) regarding the extreme velocity of the arrow. //29//
"Mārīca," and so forth.
"I perceive" means I infer:
that she is distressed by separation from me.
Existence. //30//

It should be diverted—that is, consoled. Here, because the *karuṇa* (compassion) centered on Rāma is being obscured by sentiments such as *krodha* (anger) and others, it possesses the status of a semblance (*ābhāsatva*).
As it is stated in the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*: "At the beginning and the end, [the sentiment] is doubled by those other than itself."
"Whether it be at the beginning, the middle, or [the end], if it is properly [placed], it attains the state of a semblance of rasa.
Thus, regarding "the mountain of play": because that [mountain] has been overturned, it is unfit for the movement of play; by that [fact]...
The obstruction of the spread of fame has also been mentioned.
*Vaikakṣyakam* is a garland worn across the chest; Amarasimha states: "But *vaikakṣyaka* is that which is cast obliquely across the chest" (152).
*Karaṅka* means a corpse. *Traiguṇya* (the three qualities) is accompanied by attachment to the body.
This is the dramatic element (*aṅga*) called *sambhrama* (agitation); as it has been said: "Fear, terror, and agitation constitute *sambhrama*" (153).
"O descendant of Pulastya," and so forth.
"Saṅkaṭam" means "constricted" (śliṣṭam).
"Kṣaṇonmīlitam" means "unfurled for a moment. Up to this point.
In the inner chamber,
there was first the obstruction caused by Rāvaṇa, and then the affliction of heaven.
The meaning is "there is not. A second king is a *dvirāja*;

the state of that is *dvairājyam*. According to the *Bhāṣya*: "In a compound, there is the elision of the ordinal suffix following a numeral" (Pāṇini 5.3.50). [The word is used] for the sake of the hero (*vīrāya*).
This [act] is characterized by the motive of giving;
it is the subsidiary element (*upāṅga*) known as *sandhyantara*, specifically that which is called "giving" (*dāna*).
As it has been said: "Giving is the offering of ornaments and so forth, serving as a representative of oneself. (155)
Thus [ends the thirty-first].
"Kṣaṇam" means there is no delay in the execution; such is the sense.
According to Vardhamāna, the indeclinable "diṣṭyā" is used in the sense of joy; here it is used in the sense of "hanta" (well done).
"Vardhayāmi" means I encourage or incite; this is used in the sense of proximity to the present tense.
*Laṭ*.

(157) *Vācika* means a message. (158) Regarding the phrase "synonym for friend," etc.: "friend" (*mitra*) is that which is "intervened"—that is, distinguished—by a synonym, i.e., another name. In common usage...
Among attendants, there is the state of being designated by such terms as "slave" or "servant"; however, in this case, there is this distinction:
even while practicing servitude, I [am addressed] by Your Majesty.
The meaning is: "I desire to be designated by the word *mitra*.
Thus he says, "a synonym for *mitra*," and so forth; this is further intended as a request.
*Prabhuśakti* consists of the treasury (*kośa*) and the army (*daṇḍa*). *Ādiśya* means having consecrated [him] in Kiṣkindhā.
The completeness of powers (*śakti*) refers to counsel (*mantra*) and enthusiasm (*utsāha*).
Because it was already accomplished beforehand; "the limit of enmity" means the slaying of the enemy;
and Vālin's being put to use [as an instrument] occurred at that very moment due to his having conquered Rāvaṇa.
Because he is himself capable of bringing back Sītā without depending on anyone else;
and because Sugrīva’s utility lies in his future role as a provider of treasury and army, which is contingent upon a lapse of time.
"Arrogant," and so forth.

*Kaṇḍūḥ* (itching) refers here to the itch for battle; its *bhiduraṃ* means that which breaks it [the itch]. [The suffix] *kurac* is applied after the roots *vid*, *bhid*, and *chid*. By force, he was exhaling heat (*ūṣmāṇa*).
The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied according to the rule "upon vomiting by means of steam (*bāṣpa*) or heat (*uṣman*)" (Pāṇini 3.1.16);
because the fiery heat produced by strength (*bala*) destroys itching rooted in the lunar (*saumya*) phlegm (*śleṣman*), that designation is applied to strength as well.
By way of figurative expression (upacāra):

because Rāvaṇa has been conquered and so forth, he will not seek to join forces due to his desire for what ought not to be done. Therefore, I wish to make Sugrīva himself a firmer ally through the task of slaying Vālin.
Greater firmness [of alliance] arises from being a friend in action; regarding this, Māgha says: "A friend and an enemy are both artificial;
for they exist only through their actions. (162) The son of another's wife is *pārastraiṇeya*.

By the rule *strībhyo ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.1.120), the suffix *ḍhak* is applied; in connection with that, by the inclusion of the *kalyāṇī* group, the suffix *inaṅ* is added; and by the inclusion of the *anuśatika* group, there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both parts of the compound. *Vyaya* means destruction. Therefore...
Thus, due to the unfitness for the conceit of being a son, there is a relaxation of his grief;
this is because he has propitiated Śakra by establishing his grandson Aṅgada in the position of crown prince;
he will say exactly that: "his grandson..."
Hearing also that Prince Aṅgada was [alive], the thousand-eyed Indra, out of extreme joy, became a cluster consisting of pearls in the form of a flood of droplets from his tears. (166) //32//

*Devabhūyam* means the state of being a god (*devatvam*); the suffix *kyap* is applied according to the rule *bhuvo bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.18). *Tadrūpām gatiṃ* means "a course of that nature. *Avadhātavyam* means one must remain vigilant (*apramattena sthātavyam*).
*Dūtyam* is the business of a messenger (*dūtasya karma*); the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *dūtavaṇigbhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.127).
The construction is "even as a counter-messenger.
Regarding "father" and so forth:
*retodhāḥ* means the emitter (the progenitor).
The suffix *asun* (Pāṇini 3.2.101) in the word *asun* is an *uṇādi* suffix denoting the agent; *guru* means the immutable one (*kūṭastha*),
since he is the father of Manu, the progenitor of our lineage.
And that man is your half-brother (*vaimātreya*), meaning a son of a different mother; for "a *vaimātreya* is one born of a different mother" (Amara-kośa 2.6.170).
Thus says Amara; [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule *śubhrādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.123).

Therefore (*tat*), you are a friend by nature (*sahaja*). The use of the word "also" (*api*) is because your friendship through action has already been established by your favor in sending the upper garment; indeed, even before that...

The sense is that you need not pray for the attainment of friendliness (*maitra*). *Jñāteya* means the state of being a kinsman, that is, sharing in common suffering; *kāpeyena* means by the nature of a monkey.
‘The suffix ḍhak occurs after the words kapi and jñāti’ (Pāṇini 4.1.109); *tarala* means fickle; *śithilayasi* means you do not share [the burden of] suffering.
The ellipsis is "due to the suspicion that I might not be favorably disposed.
That being so (*tat* = *tarhi*), if I am to show you favor,
let my arrows be the means for accomplishing your desired purpose.
"Guarantors" (*pratibhuvaḥ*) means *lagnakas*. By the words "the son of Vali," etc., he indicates the benefit [of the alliance],
and by the phrase "if you were ungrateful, then I would kill you too," he points out the undesirable consequence (*bādha*) in the opposing case.
The sense is that although there may not be an equality of suffering with a kinsman, it could nonetheless arise from the act of killing Vālin. //33//

"By which [woman]" refers back to the meaning of the preceding verse. By the words "constantly" and so forth, he indicates that he, being one who has duties to perform, nevertheless possesses a longing born of affection. "I am highly favored" means: when you have made your request, I shall grant it to you.
Because it was given by Maitra, it is an act of supreme favor. Guha’s laughter arises from superimposing upon the sun later on the specific quality of being unbearable; this is his joy.
Due to obtaining the favor of Sugrīva, his own desired object;
from this point until "śriyaṃ raviḥ" (173),
[the section] is named *dūtī*.
The subordinate element (*upāṅga*) called *sandhyantara*; as it has been said: "But the role of a messenger is the state of being an auxiliary in a task that is difficult to accomplish.
[This refers to] Sugrīva and so forth; [it denotes] partiality.
From the giving of friendship—by that partiality—what is the gain for us, i.e., for ourselves? But rather, it is for the Sun alone; such is the sense. Let him know (vidāṅkarotu) = let him understand.
Regarding the rule *vidāṅkurvantv ity anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.41),
the *Kāśikā* states: "There is indeed a restriction regarding the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*), but not a restriction regarding the singular number and so forth."
*Rabhasa* is excitement.
(34) (177) Regarding "how," and so forth: the term *aṅgīkāritāḥ* refers back to the meaning of the second half-verse.
"How?"—this expresses wonder regarding his skill in speech.
"Openly" (*prakāśam*) means by way of the literal sense (*vācyavṛttyā*). "Thus" (*evam*) refers to the granting of the kingdom.
"Does not wish to promise" (*na pratiśuśrūṣati*) means he does not desire to agree; [this is based on the rule] *jñā-śru-smṛ-dṛśām...* [Pāṇini 1.3.57].
Regarding the *ātmanepada* [ending] in "sanaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.62), there is a prohibition by the rule "pratyāṅbhyāṃ śruvaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.59). [The suffix] *icchā*.
"Tvasti" means "as far as.

*Śailī* means "the state of being a stone" (*śailyam*); the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class (Pāṇini 5.1.124), and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because of the presence of *ṣ* (Pāṇini 4.1.41), according to the rule "halastaddhitasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.150).
Thus, there is the elision of the letter *y*.
Regarding the phrase "the virtuous" (*santaḥ*) and so forth:
it means having brought to mind—that is, intending—rather than having explicitly stated; [this is because of the rule] "not when there is no placing upon" (*anatyādhāna*).

In the phrase "urasimanasī" (on the chest and in the mind), the suffix *lyap* is applied because these are words denoting motion (*gati*). Regarding "kṛtye" = that which is to be done, and "vastuni" = the matter/task:
for whom (*kasya* = for whom) did he promise the fortune (*śrī*) whose recipient was Kamala?
The genitive case is used here to express a general relationship; otherwise, [it would have been different].

Because of the rule "the term *kriyā* (action) must be included," the fourth case (*caturthī*) would apply due to [the recipient] being the *sampradāna*. The meaning is: "having set out without having made a promise.
Or else: before whom? To whom did he promise glory for the sake of the lotuses?
By the rule "pratyāṅbhyāṃ śruvaḥ pūrvasya kartā" (Pāṇini 1.4.40), [the agent of the preceding action] receives the status of the recipient (sampradāna). //35//

Regarding "dundubhikaraṅka," and so forth: *avaṣṭambha* means pride (*garva*). In the absence of the ego-inflation of heroism, even this throwing of the skull-bowl (*karaṅkavikṣepa*), which has been thus prohibited, does not occur.
The sense is that he should act [in such a way]. He will remove [it]; the sense is "by means of battle.
Regarding "I think" and so forth: they are "possessed of disease" (*āmayavantau*) due to pride as the illness; here the suffix is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*).

The suffix *vini* is applied by the rule "the addition of *amaya* is prescribed everywhere" (Pāṇini 5.2.128); the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "it is seen in other cases as well" (Pāṇini 6.3.137). [The word] *dorbhyām* [is used] in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthambhāva-lakṣaṇe*).
Third:
(190) "Not only has he always been unable to endure anything out of pride, but today he is especially so."
"Enflamed" means blazing with anger; the construction is to be understood as "I think [this] because of Jāmbavat’s instigation. //36//
*Vīrayātrā* means war. Regarding the phrase "prepared" (*praklṛptā*) and so forth:
it was prepared by Janaka, that is, by his father.

*Kāntārakumārāḥ* means forest-dwellers; *bhuktiḥ* is the enjoyment or possession of which belongs to them, for they subsist on bulbs, roots, and the like. Alternatively, the forest itself is the "enjoyment of the princes" (*kumārabhoga*); for kings [assign] it for the sake of the enjoyment of their own princes.
They divide [the inheritance] such as villages and so forth, but for him, in that place, there is only the forest. Having done thus, it was "muktaḥ" = abandoned.
It is the offspring (*apatyam*) of one who is "durbhagāyāḥ" = devoid of fortune; the suffix *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule beginning with "kalyāṇī" (Pāṇini 4.1.126).

By conjunction with that [suffix], there is also the substitution of *anaṅ* for the final vowel; furthermore, by the rule "hṛdbhaga" (Pāṇini 7.3.192), there is vṛddhi strengthening of both members of the compound. Otherwise, [the form would not apply] even in the case of "priyāyām premṇā" or "tatputre."
The meaning is that there should be affection (*vātsalya*).
A *sāmanta* is a minor king. //37//
"By means of a *paṭaccara*—that is, by means of a worn-out garment belonging to a traveler;
one who lives by such [garments] is a *pāṭaccara*, meaning a thief;
[the phrase refers to] that which belongs to him. *Ātiṣṭhamānau* means they accepted it; [from the root] *āṅ*..."
The suffix *taṅ* (the ātmanepada endings) is applied by the rule "sthaḥ pratijñāne" (Pāṇini 1.3.22).
"tad" and so forth.
"These two" refers to those pointed out by Rāvaṇa.
"O long-lived one" is used in address; "address" means censure, born of folly. That [is it].

Because his status as a Kṣatriya was revealed without doubt; the meaning is that by his appearance, only his being a Kṣatriya is known, but not his specific identity. Unable to tolerate this, Lakṣmaṇa said: "O fool, you yourself are one who fails to discern even the specific distinction explicitly stated in the word 'the two Rāghavas'."
With this intention, he says: "But has it not already been stated? The word *nanu* indicates what is well-known;
the meaning is that it has indeed been clearly stated. Thus, he attributes to that very [subject] the very same delusion that was superimposed upon himself.
He spoke with anger: "Āḥ! Wretch," and so forth. *Āḥ* is used in the sense of pain; as it is said: "*Āstu* may be used in [the senses of] anger and pain" (194).
Thus says Amara;
the word *api* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). *Vivṛṇoti* means "he speaks"; the sense is, "what does he say? Furthermore, the ellipsis is:
"we do not perceive that very distinction by which (*yena*) you speak again and again."
*Sāṃskārika* means "derived from the sacrament of naming" (*nāmakaraṇa-saṃskāra*); [the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *tata āgataḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.74).
*Niścinomi* means "I would determine"; [the suffix] *liṅ* is applied according to the rule *vibhāṣā kathaṃ liṅ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.143).
The meaning is as follows: unambiguous Kṣatriya-hood is not the subject of the question;
rather, it is that which is excluded [from other categories].
"It is merely a name;

how then could I determine it by means of the suffix *aṇ* which signifies 'offspring'?"—the exclamation "Ah! expresses the distress caused by the failure to mention the specific point he wished to know. //38//

Lakṣmaṇa’s composure and agitation [arise] because Vālin’s words were preceded by resentment; *saṃrambha* means anger. These two [qualities] are well known; by this, he indicates [Lakṣmaṇa’s] breaking of Śiva’s bow, his victory over the son of Jamadagni, and so forth. This...
The ornament known as *leśa* (the suggestive); it has been said: "A *leśa* is speech possessing a qualifying attribute that brings about the knowledge of an intention" (197).

*Damayitā* means a breaker or subduer. Regarding the phrase "he might be Rāma": the construction is that he, who is denoted by the word "Rāma," is the well-known Rāmabhadra. The particle *api* expresses possibility (*sambhāvanā*), while *kim* expresses deliberation (*vitarka*).
"One," and so forth.
"Dress" (*veṣa*) refers to bark garments and the like. "One" (*eka*) means uniform or indistinguishable.
"Of actions" (*karmaṇām*) refers to battles and the like; "equipment" (*parikara*) means the instruments, such as the bow and so forth.
“Common” (sādhāraṇaḥ) means equal (tulyaḥ). “Sweetness” (madhuratvam) means being dear (priyatvam), which is indeed similar.

“Profundity” (gambhīratā) means invincibility (adhṛṣyatā). “Again” (punar)—that is to say, even though he has laid down his weapons (sannyastaśastraḥ). He is one who has girded his loins for the slaughter of all Kṣatriyas. “He has been made a transgressor” (avakīrṇī)—meaning one whose vow has been broken (kṣatavrataḥ); that is to say, he has been conquered (jitaḥ).
The vow has been violated—that is, scattered—by him;
[the suffix] *ini* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.88 (*iṣṭādibhyaśca*).
Since the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) could have been established by the suffix *ini*, [the rule is stated as it is].
This injunction is for the purpose of excluding others; Amara states that "one who has spilled his seed" (*avakīrṇin*) is "one whose vow is broken" (*kṣatavrata*).
The construction is: "Which [of these] is that Rāmabhadra? //39//
The Vinaya is so called because it is praised; for this very reason, there is the expression "Āryā.

As for the phrase "Lakṣmaṇa, for his part" (*lakṣmaṇas tāvat*): the meaning of the word *tāvat* is a delay, intended to indicate that one is pointing out Rāma by means of the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). Because of the elder brother's status as a guru, he is not mentioned directly.
The statement "it is fitting" is made by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).
Vālin’s joy and exultation arise from obtaining a worthy rival warrior.
Regarding the passage beginning with "this one," there are three [verses].
*Varṇāḥ* refers to the three castes (*traivarṇyam*), with the suffix *ṣyañ* added in the sense of the base itself according to the rule for *cāturvarṇya* and similar compounds.
That very thing—merely the state of being the three castes (*traivarṇyamātram*). According to the rule, "*Mātraṃ* [is used] in the sense of totality or restriction. (201–202)

Thus says Amara. In that very place, by him the world was "concluded" (*avasitam*)—that is, brought to an end—meaning that all the kṣatriyas were slain. [He took her] from the womb (*garbhāt*), that is, from the belly.
"Drawn forth" means removed; because birth is eternal, its production is not mentioned.
(203) You have been heard of before; the meaning is that today you have become the subject of conversation. Therefore, it is a "fair dawn"; today—
The meaning is that "auspicious" refers to the characteristic of awakening. *Āsphoṭa* means battle;
as Amara states: "Kalahā, āsphoṭa, and saṃyuga [are synonyms for battle]. (204)

That which has that as its object is "itching" (*kaṇḍū*), just like the physical sensation of itch; it is "itching" because it has a harsh itch as its object, owing to its being the cause of scratching; that very thing is the "disorder" (*vikāra*), that is, the disease.
The power of heat-induced sweat to destroy itching is stated in the verse beginning with "dṛpyatpaulastya" (205). Among heroes,
*śrāddha* means one who possesses faith (*śraddhāvān*).

The sense is: "May he please you, the hero, with battle"; the suffix *ṇa* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), according to the rule beginning with *prajñā-śraddhā* (Pāṇini 5.2.101). //40//
"By whom," and so forth;
"by the Hero" contains the reason [for his action]; "the Earth" refers to the deity presiding over it.
Elsewhere, being oppressed by Rāvaṇa, she dispels her sorrow in a corner of Kiṣkindhā;
that is to say, she remains there because she cannot be reached by Rāvaṇa. //41//
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the gods and asuras" (*surāsurāṇām*),
here, because they have immortality as their goal, there is no application of the rule for forming a singular compound according to Pāṇini 2.4.9: *yeṣāṃ ca virodhaḥ śāśvatikaḥ*.
Because opposition is not eternal;

or [the compound] *surayuktā asurāḥ* may be analyzed with the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopa*), since it belongs to the class of compounds beginning with *śākapārthiva*. Regarding the word *asubhiḥ*, [it is derived from] *divaḥ*...

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the action" (*karma ca*), the designation of the instrument (*karaṇa-saṃjñā*) is indicated; thus, the form *krīḍatām* (of those playing) also resonates [as the instrumental]. The *sabhika* is the guarantor (*pratibhū*), the one who initiates the gambling; this is because Nārada is fond of quarreling.
"Gamblers are those who play with dice," according to Amara; "within the range of the serpent" is a statement made with pride. //42//
In battle, "śauṇḍa" means intoxicated— that is to say, unrestrained.
"O King," and so forth.
"Crushed" means afflicted. "Bonds in the form of braids" [are so called] due to the absence of refinement (*saṃskāra*). "Continuous" means uninterrupted.
(213) *Sidhmādi-laḥ*: [The suffix] *la* is applied after words such as *sidhma*.
(214) *Prasṛmara* means "pervading" (*vyāpta*); [it is derived from] *sṛ*, *ghas*, and *sad* with the suffix *kmarac*.
(215) *Uḍḍāmara* means "frightening. Regarding *rajyat-*: [it is derived from] *kuṣi* and *rañj* [with the suffix *kyuṭ*].

By the use of [the suffixes] *śyan* and the *parasmaipada* ending in such passages, there is praise in the phrase "the son of Mahāvīra" because his eyes were red with anger even while capturing the celestial damsels as captives; yet, there is also censure in the sense that he is "the son of one who is not a hero. //43//
"Having made [it] captive," and so forth. "Difficult to traverse" means it is a place difficult to enter;
"unconquerable" is the sense, [meaning] by Indra and the other gods—this is the ellipsis.
Even though there is an abundance of pillars...
It becomes difficult to enter during the twilight.
Samādhi is one-pointedness; that itself is the vow (vrata), which is the restraint (niyama); for a vow is indeed [defined] according to the scriptures.
The rule is as follows:
(216) because even those seeking a vulnerability cannot be harmed when the time for their execution has arrived, they are taken captive;
"having released" means having abandoned them. Here, the "queens" are the rivers. By the second half [of the verse]:

The disclosure of the breach in the uniqueness of Vālin’s prowess: It is said that in former times, Arjuna went to the Revā river; desiring to sport, he blocked the waters of the Narmadā with his thousand arms for the sake of filling [his pool]. At that time—

The story should be understood as follows: while Rāvaṇa was performing his devotions on its bank, his ritual observances were interrupted by a surging flood of water; consequently, out of anger, he fought with Kārtavīrya and was defeated. (217) This is the wonder of the oceans: that even on their own shores, they have conquered all the worlds.
There is an absence of wonder because of the first sight of the Rākṣasa’s defeat, and because of seeing Narmadā— who has herself conquered Rāvaṇa— and yet another.
"Conqueror of Rāvaṇa" is a praise; however, since he shared that title with Kārtavīrya, it is a censure. //44//
"May it be long," and so forth.
"Night-walkers" (*rātriñcarāḥ*) refers to *rākṣasas*; the suffix *mum* is applied according to the rule *rātreḥ kṛti vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.3.72). "The wheel" (*cakram*) means the army.
*Māraḥ* = death;
*aṅke* = in battle;
*vaijñānikaḥ* = skilled; "a *vaijñānikaḥ* is one who has mastered [the art], one who is proficient (*kṛtī*)."
"Kuśala" also means "virtuous," according to Amara. "Sadharmām" means "similar"; [this is derived] from the rule: *dharmādanic kevalāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.124).
Thus [it is] "insatiable"; that is to say, the longing to see and hear has not yet ceased even now. //45//
In that case, one might ask: "Let him then be followed. To this he says:

"But, by which... and so forth. "By which" means by which state (*dhāman*); "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) means strength. The meaning is that there is no king whose strength is equal to that of the bow. "Having severed" means having seized.
By "utsargeṇa" (in general), that is, by way of the common rule for the *kula* [suffix], she is established as defeated—meaning, she has been vanquished.

Regarding the word "trayī": the suffix *ayac* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.43 (*dvitribhyāṃ tayasyāyaj vā*), and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added according to 4.1.15 (*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*) and so forth.

The meaning is "that which wards off the suffering of the three worlds. The statement "these two" is made while pointing them out. *Uttāmyataḥ* means they long for [it]; the verbal root is *tamu* in the sense of longing (Dhātupāṭha 2.23). //46//
"Indeed, this... and so forth.
*Adhimaurvikam* means "having the string fastened," according to the rule *nady-ṛtaś-ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.153), which prescribes the suffix *kap*.

*Yuddham eva sarvasvam* means that the battle itself is the "all-in-all"—the object of supreme affection and the very substance; that [battle] alone is the *dakṣiṇā*, the sacrificial fee or gift to be given. He who possesses this...
That [battle], which is the very essence of all warfare— meaning it is skillful, noble, or rather, that which bestows victory as its fruit— is the root, the cause,
for you who favor Rāvaṇa.
The meaning is that it is destructive. //47//
"According to dharma" means without transgressing dharma; here, "dharma" refers specifically to an attack against one who is armed. (226)
"naya" and so forth: *naya* means *dharma*.
*Ayaḥkuśī* is an iron product;
the word *kuśa* [is used] in the sense of an iron product.

By the rule "jānapada" (Pāṇini 4.1.42), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in usage similar to the word *karikalabha*. *Talāḥ* means palms of the hands; as Amarasimha states: "The word *tala* is not feminine when meaning 'the surface' or 'the palm'. //48//
The "transverse birth" refers to animals and the like.
Regarding the phrase "the entire flood," and so forth:
by the "flowing forth of the entire flood," meaning by an expedition equipped with all military arrays; for "the entire mobilization" (*sarvābhisāra*) is the "entire flood" (*sarvaugha*).

According to Amarasimha, [the word *sannahana*] has the meaning "all-encompassing armor" (*sarvasannahanārthaka*). Furthermore, the word *prasara* is grammatically correct by virtue of the rule *uṇādayo bahulam*.
And the application [of the argument] by Bhaṭṭācārya is as follows: "For as long as monkeys do not find a way to spread anywhere, nor do demons rush into their own domain. (232)
Thus: *sthemā* means strength (*bala*). According to the rule "priyasthira...
(Pāṇini 6.4.157), the word *sthira* undergoes the substitution *sthā* when the suffix *iman* is added. Gautama cursed Indra, who was the lover of Ahalyā, saying, "Become devoid of manliness."
The narrative is to be continued;
here, the *Mahābhārata* states: "O evil-minded one, because you have performed this improper act by assuming my form, you shall become powerless. Thus [ends] the infamy.
Because of fleeing; that which was said, "he made [the earth] share in that," is purified in the pit.
For the crab (kulīra) hides (līyate);

"dart" (śalya) refers to suffering, used metaphorically because it produces that [suffering]. Upon the victory over his own father, he becomes free from darts (viśalyatva) due to the victory over his father's [former] father. //49// (236)
"So too" (*so'pi*): the particle *api* is used here in the sense of possibility. "By fate" (*daivena*) means by fortune;
Amara states: "Fate (*daiva*), destiny (*diṣṭa*), and lot (*bhāgadheya*) [are synonyms].
Vālin’s anger arose from the disclosure of his father’s defeat.

"asmad" and so forth: the arms' quality of scraping the base of the armpits (*kakṣāmūlakūlaṅkaṣatva*) is due to their unevenly knotted nature; [the suffix] *khac* is applied by the rule "sarvakūla" (Pāṇini 3.2.42).

There is the consequence of collapse due to being squeezed out. Fame alone is one's entire possession; that itself is the *dāya*—the object to be given—which belongs to him. The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.19 (*akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*). [The word] *dāya* [also occurs] in the sense of giving.
"Regarding property such as a wedding dowry and paternal wealth"— thus says the *Vaijayantī*.
(240) *Khalacurī* was the city of Arjuna.

The state of being "sluggish" (mandāyamānatva) results from the destruction of [his] uniqueness. The sense is that even Arjuna was defeated by Rāvaṇa; thus, you—who have conquered those who conquered both Arjuna and Bhārgava—are the one to be defeated.
*Dunoti* means it causes affliction (*kleśayati*). //50//
The *pārṣṇigrāha* is the rear enemy.
(241) *Vaikartani* means the son of the Sun; [as it is said: "Vikartana, Arka, Mārtaṇḍa. (242)
Thus says Amara:
*skandhāvāra* means an army.
(243) Regarding the passage beginning with "by the curse of Brahmā" and so forth: it is said that in former times, Āñjaneya, immediately upon birth...
Thus, as the sun was rising,
wishing to eat with the thought that it was fruit, he was dissuaded by him and turned back,
desecrating the sacrificial implements in the hermitages of the sages while being watched by those sages.

The meaning is that he remained indifferent due to ignorance of his own power; the implication is that there is nothing impossible for one who possesses such knowledge. //51//

*Kauśalyā* [is derived] from *kauśalya*; from the word *kuśala*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied according to the rule "guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ karmaṇi ca" (Pāṇini 5.1.124), and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule "ṣidgaurādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.41).
A "dart" (śalya) refers to suffering as well as iron spikes and the like. By this, the extraction of the dart from Lakṣmaṇa’s heart through the subsequent bringing of Mount Droṇa is indicated.

"By his life-breaths," and so forth. (249) *Puṣkarāṇi* means lotuses. The meaning is that he offered up both his life-breaths and the garland.
*Kūlamudvahāḥ* means spreading forth beyond the shore; [the quarters]... diśaḥ.

The meaning is that they have filled [the space] and even extended upwards; [the suffix] *khaś* is applied according to the rule "udikūle rujivahoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.31). *Vīraśayana* refers to the battlefield. //52//

*Śātakumbha* means *kārtasvara*, gold. From this point until the end of the passage beginning with "dear beyond dear to us" (251), [the text describes] the seed (*bīja*)— consisting of Rāma's resolve— which resides in the *garbhasandhi* (embryonic juncture), by means of Sugrīva’s consecration.
Because it consists in directing [the plot] toward the primary matter at hand, it is the constituent element named *ākṣepa* (suggestion/anticipation).

As it has been said: "Suggestion (*ākṣepa*) is proclaimed as the drawing forth of the seed of the *garbha* [sandhi]" (252). Here, "drawing forth" (*samutkṣepaḥ*) means [directing it] toward the primary matter.

The term "deposit" (nikṣepa) is used because he adorns [her] himself; this is an expression of respect. His dearness is established through both the warding off of what is undesirable and the protection of what is desired.
He is called "Great King" (mahārāja) because of his consecration.

*Ūrdhvamauhūrtike* means "occurring after a *muhūrta*"; it is analyzed as "that which occurs after (*ūrdhvam*) a *muhūrta*."

by the rule "and *liṅ* in the sense of 'lasting for more than a moment' (*ūrdhvamauhūrtika*)," there is a compound formation and the vṛddhi strengthening of the final member.
"The word *ūrdhvamauhūrtika* here is used in the sense of proximity to the present time," according to the *Nyāsa*.

She is one who possesses *dvairājyam*—the state of being ruled by two kings (*dvirājā*); the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied according to the rule beginning with "guṇavacana" (Pāṇini 5.1.124). Thus, *vairāgyam* refers to the world-weariness born from mutual strife between two kings; she is one who has that [state].
By the word *daivataṃ*, it is indicated that he possesses long-lasting stability like Indra and other deities.

*Naptāraṃ* means a grandson (*pautraṃ*).
Having heard of the crown prince, [his eyes] shone like clusters of pearls because they were drenched with tears of joy; and that was due to his having a thousand eyes. //54//

"More dear than the dear": because by installing Aṅgada, they avoided the offense against Indra that would have resulted from installing Sugrīva. "Sharing together" (*saṃvibhāginau*): having divided [the kingdom].

Regarding the term "mark" (*aṅka*): its status as a "mark" arises because it is not directly perceived as an operation, being separated from the primary matter at hand—the bringing back of Sītā—by the intermediate matter consisting of the slaying of Vālin.
Because it is connected with the *bindu* (the essential point) expressed by the phrase "to seek news of Queen Sītā" (260),
[it serves as] the *vāli* that conceals the fault consisting in the killing of Vālin, who was without offense.
And because it serves as the locus for the heroic, the furious, the pathetic, and the erotic sentiments through various arrangements such as the plotting of the protagonist's pursuit.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Anargharāghava-pañcikā* composed by Viṣṇu, son of Muktinātha.
